title: Accepting the will
hook: bhaana is sweet acceptance of what the Lord sends

segments.voice: Yesterday, death without fear: whoever has come will go, and the one who remembers the fearless One need not be ruled by fear. Your line was unafraid. Which small fear did you take the wheel back from? Day one thousand three hundred ninety-four.

Tera keeya meetha laagai. A short line in Gurmukhi, from a hymn of Guru Arjan in Raag Asa. Your doing seems sweet to me. Sikhs sing the line in kirtan, and it's easy to hum it without hearing how bold it is. It doesn't say, your doing is easy. It doesn't say, your doing is what I wanted. It says sweet. About whatever comes. Tradition ties the line to Guru Arjan's own last days, which were anything but sweet. Today's word is the inner turn that makes a line like that possible: bhaana.
screen: `TERA KEEYA MEETHA LAAGAI.` → `YOUR DOING SEEMS SWEET TO ME.` → `BHAANA.`

segments.voice: First, the word. Bhaana is the will of the Lord, what pleases the Lord, the way things come to us. Sikhs speak of bhaana mannana: accepting the will. It sits close to Hukam, the order we've met many times. Hukam is the order itself; bhaana is that order arriving in your own life, on an ordinary day, as news you didn't ask for. Second, the line in full. The hymn goes on, in paraphrase: your doing seems sweet to me; Nanak asks for the treasure of the Lord's Name. Notice what's being asked for. Not a different outcome. The Name. The prayer turns from changing what happened to staying close to the One it came from. Third, the hardest part: the story. Tradition says Guru Arjan was tortured in Lahore and died there, and that through it he kept repeating this very line. Sikhs remember that as bhaana at its hardest: not a calm man in a calm room, but a man in agony, still saying sweet. Fourth, what bhaana is not. It isn't giving up. The same tradition that tells Guru Arjan's story then tells how his son, the Sixth Guru, took up arms. Sikhs feed the hungry, stand against injustice, go to the doctor, fix what can be fixed. Bhaana is about the heart's stance toward what has already come, not an excuse to stop acting on what still can change. So accepting the will is not a shrug. It's taking what arrived, even bitter, and refusing to let it push the Lord out of the room.
screen: `BHAANA: THE WILL, ARRIVING.` · `NOT A NEW OUTCOME, BUT THE NAME.` · `GURU ARJAN, STILL SAYING SWEET.` · `NOT A SHRUG; STILL ACTING.` · then, large: `TERA KEEYA MEETHA LAAGAI.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: accept one thing today. Settle, and breathe. Bring to mind one thing you've been resisting that you truly cannot change. Not an injustice you could act on; something that has simply happened. A delay. A no. A body that's slower than it was. On the in-breath, name it. On the out-breath, try the word accepted, and see if any part of you can loosen around it. Sweet may be too far today; lighter is enough. If you pray, you can hum the Guru's line, tera keeya meetha laagai. The bell holds the time.
Bhaana. The will of the Lord, as it arrives in a life; bhaana mannana is accepting it, sweetly, while still doing what can be done. Today's word.

Your line: his will. Today, when one small thing goes against your plan, before you push back, pause and say inside: his will. Then decide what, if anything, is yours to do. Day one thousand three hundred ninety-four.

howItsDone: Sikhs speak of bhaana mannana, accepting the Lord's will, especially in loss; the shabad tera keeya meetha laagai is often sung in kirtan, and Sikhs recall it in connection with Guru Arjan's martyrdom.

fork.reveal: bhaana accepts what has come without becoming a shrug; the same tradition tells of the Sixth Guru taking up arms.

original.note: Gurmukhi: the will, what pleases the Lord; bhaana mannana is to accept it.

trapdoor: what you thought: accepting God's will means being passive.
what it means: bhaana is meeting what comes without letting it push the Lord out of the heart, while still acting.
what a scholar hears: Guru Arjan's Asa hymn, tera keeya meetha laagai, asks only for the Name, and tradition ties it to his martyrdom in Lahore.
